property_summary: For any caller and setup, the correct contract's owner() returns the stored owner address (the deployer initialized via __Ownable_init), whereas the mutant returns tx.origin which can differ from the stored owner for some callers (so owner() should equal the stored _owner, but mutant breaks this for some tx.origin).

For any caller address X, the deployed correct contract's owner() always returns the stored owner (the deployer), i.e. owner() == deployer regardless of msg.sender; the mutant returns tx.origin which can differ from the stored owner when the call is proxied through another caller, so under a proxied call from a fuzzed caller address the mutant's owner() can differ and thus violates the rule.

For any caller (tx.origin and msg.sender arbitrary), the reference contract's owner() always equals the deployer address (the stored owner); the mutant returns tx.origin instead, so when a call is proxied through another contract (tx.origin != deployer) the mutant's owner() can differ and thus violate the rule.

For every caller (including when the call is proxied through another contract), the reference C.owner() always returns the deployer (the stored owner); the mutant returns tx.origin, so when a fuzzed external EOA calls a proxy contract which then calls C.owner(), the mutant's return (tx.origin) can differ from the stored owner and thus violate this rule.

For every call, the genuine contract's owner() always returns the stored owner (the deployer set during initialization); the mutant that returns tx.origin can produce a different address when owner() is invoked via a proxy contract so the property (owner() == deployer) is violated for some proxied calls.

For any nonzero newOwner address, transferOwnership(newOwner) always succeeds on the reference and leaves owner() equal to newOwner; the mutant additionally allows newOwner == address(0) which results in owner() == address(0) for some inputs (i.e. transferring ownership to zero is permitted by the mutant but forbidden by the reference).

The reference contract rejects transferring ownership to the zero address (transferOwnership(address(0)) reverts) for every input, whereas the mutant allows it (transferOwnership(address(0)) succeeds and owner() becomes address(0)) for some input; the test fuzzes the newOwner and checks that calling transferOwnership with that address never succeeds when newOwner == address(0).

For all newOwner addresses, the reference contract never allows setting owner() to the zero address (transferOwnership(address(0)) reverts), while the mutant permits transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed and makes owner() == address(0) for that input.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) in the reference either reverts when newOwner==address(0) or results in owner() equal to newOwner; the mutant allows the call to succeed with newOwner==address(0) and thus can make owner() == address(0) while the reference never does, so the property asserts that transferOwnership(address(0)) must never succeed (call must revert) when invoked by the current owner.

The reference contract always reverts when the current owner attempts to transfer ownership to the zero address (transferOwnership(address(0)) fails), whereas the mutant allows transferring ownership to address(0) (call succeeds) — so for all callers equal to owner(), transferOwnership(newOwner) must revert iff newOwner == address(0).

Invariant: calling transferOwnership(newOwner) as the current owner always succeeds (does not revert) for any newOwner address (including the current owner) on the reference contract; the mutant introduces a require that reverts when newOwner is the same as the current owner, so some inputs (newOwner == current owner) will make the call revert there.

For any address newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) as the current owner never reverts on the reference C; the mutant adds a check that reverts when newOwner equals the current owner, so some inputs (newOwner == current owner) will make the call revert.

For any address newOwner, when called by the current owner transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference C never reverts (it allows no-op transfers); the mutant adds a require(newOwner != _owner) causing the call to revert if newOwner equals the current owner — so there exists an input (newOwner == current owner) that makes the mutant revert while the reference does not.

For any address candidateNewOwner, when called by the current owner the reference C never reverts transferring ownership to candidateNewOwner (including when candidateNewOwner equals the current owner), whereas the mutant may revert when candidateNewOwner equals the current owner; we assert that calling transferOwnership(candidateNewOwner) as the current owner never reverts on the reference.

For any address newOwner and when called by the current owner, the original contract allows transferOwnership(newOwner) to succeed (including when newOwner == current owner); the mutant adds a require(newOwner != _owner) causing the call to revert for inputs where newOwner equals the current owner.
For every call, paused() must return the actual internal pause flag _paused (i.e. paused() == _paused); the mutant inverts this and thus for some inputs paused() will return the opposite value.

For every input (whether caller is owner/keeper/other and any timing), the reference contract's paused() returns the actual pause state (_paused); the mutant flips the returned boolean, so there exist inputs where paused() != _paused and thus paused()'s value differs between reference and mutant.

For every input the reference contract returns the actual paused state (paused() == _paused); the mutant inverts the return and thus there exist inputs where paused() from the contract differs (paused() != _paused).

For any caller and any input address _keeper, calling setKeeper(_keeper) on the correct contract sets keeper() equal to the provided _keeper (i.e. keeper is updated to the argument); the mutant breaks this by always setting keeper() to address(0) regardless of the argument.

For any caller address, the owner-only setter setKeeper can only be successfully called by the contract owner (i.e. calls by non-owners revert / fail); the mutant inverts the onlyOwner check allowing non-owners to succeed and thus change keeper for some caller addresses.

For every caller address, in the correct contract a non-owner call to setKeeper(address) must revert (only the owner may change keeper), whereas the mutant inverts the check allowing some non-owner caller to successfully change keeper — so there exists a caller address and newKeeper input for which the mutant's setKeeper succeeds but the reference reverts.

For any caller and proposed new keeper address, the reference C allows setKeeper to succeed only when called by the contract owner; the mutant incorrectly allows some non-owner callers to succeed and thus can change keeper for inputs where the reference reverts.

For every caller address and proposed new keeper, the reference contract only allows setKeeper to succeed when called by the contract owner (calls by non-owners always revert), while the mutant inverts the onlyOwner check and thus there exist non-owner callers and new-keeper inputs for which setKeeper succeeds and changes keeper.

For every caller and proposed new keeper address, the original contract only allows setKeeper to succeed when called by the contract owner; the mutant inverts the onlyOwner check and therefore there exist non-owner callers and new-keeper inputs for which setKeeper succeeds (changing keeper) while the reference would revert.

For any uint256 x passed to setThresholds(x), the contract's stored slippageThresholdGmxBps equals exactly the passed value x after the call; the mutant that adds 1 breaks this for any x where x != x+1 (i.e. for all x), so the mutant will produce a different stored value for some inputs.

For any uint256 input x that fits in uint16 (0..10000), calling setThresholds(x) stores slippageThresholdGmxBps equal to x (reference) but the mutant that adds 1 will store a different value for any x where x+1 != x (i.e. most x), so there exists x in the admissible domain where stored value differs; the test asserts stored value equals the passed-in value.

For any admissible threshold t in [0, MAX_BPS-1] the reference stores slippageThresholdGmxBps == t after setThresholds(t); the mutant that adds 1 will store a different value for at least one admissible t (breaking the equality).

For any uint256 input t that is a valid basis-points threshold (0..10000), calling setThresholds(t) should make c.slippageThresholdGmxBps() equal to t; the mutant that adds 1 breaks this by storing t+1 for some inputs.

For any input t in 0..10000 (valid BPS), calling setThresholds(t) results in slippageThresholdGmxBps() being <= 10000 and equal to the value passed (the reference stores exactly t within valid BPS bounds); the mutant that adds 1 will store t+1 which can exceed 10000 when t==10000, breaking the property that stored value is <=10000 for that input.
For any uint256 input x, after calling setThresholds(x) the contract's slippageThresholdGmxBps equals the provided input x; the mutant that always sets it to zero violates this for any x != 0.

For any uint256 input t passed to setThresholds(t), the reference contract stores that exact value in slippageThresholdGmxBps (c.slippageThresholdGmxBps() == t); the mutant that unconditionally writes zero will violate this whenever t != 0.

For any uint256 input t, after calling setThresholds(t) by the contract owner, the stored slippageThresholdGmxBps equals t; the mutant that always assigns zero will cause the stored value to differ for some t (any t != 0).
For any owner-invoked setThresholds(x), the contract's public slippageThresholdGmxBps value equals the provided x; the mutant that always writes zero breaks this when x != 0.

For any uint256 newBps provided by the owner, after calling setThresholds(newBps) the contract's public slippageThresholdGmxBps must be greater-or-equal-to zero and equal to the provided value when the caller is the owner; the mutant that always assigns zero will cause c.slippageThresholdGmxBps() != newBps for some non-zero newBps (violating the equality).

For any input _slippageThresholdGmxBps, calling setThresholds(...) sets the contract's slippageThresholdGmxBps state to exactly the provided argument; the mutant breaks this by always setting it to 10000 for some inputs.

For any admissible slippage value x in [0,10000], calling setThresholds(x) results in c.slippageThresholdGmxBps() == x (the reference preserves the input); the mutant breaks this by forcing the stored value to 10000 for some inputs.
